title: A Servant Prayed for a Sign Beside a Well. Before He Finished Praying, She Appeared.
paragraphs: A Servant Prayed for a Sign Beside a Well. Before He Finished Praying, She Appeared.
Isaac and Rebekah, the prayer God was already answering, and the terrifying beauty of trusting Him when you cannot see what He is arranging.
He was still praying.
That is the detail I cannot get past.
Not the camels.
Not the jewelry.
Not even the young woman walking toward the well with a jar resting on her shoulder.
The prayer.
Because Genesis does not say Abraham's servant prayed, went home, waited three months, and eventually discovered that God had heard him.
It says something far more breathtaking.
The Hebrew of Genesis 24:15 reads:
וַיְהִי־הוּא טֶרֶם כִּלָּה לְדַבֵּר וְהִנֵּה רִבְקָה יֹצֵאת
Vayehi-hu terem killah ledabber, vehinneh Rivqah yotzet...
“And it came to pass, before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah came out...”
Before he finished.
Read that again slowly.
Before he finished.
The servant was still forming words while the answer to those words was already walking toward him.
He did not know her name.
He did not know her family.
He did not know whether she would stop.
He could not see what God had been arranging beyond the horizon of his understanding.
All he knew was that Abraham had sent him on what must have felt like an enormous assignment: travel back toward Abraham's relatives and find a wife for Isaac.
Not just anybody.
The woman who would become Isaac's wife would enter the covenant family through which God's promises to Abraham would continue.
And the servant understood something that many of us learn only after exhausting ourselves:
Some assignments are too large for human cleverness.
So beside a well, far from home, he prayed.
“LORD, God of my master Abraham...”

He asked God to show chesed—חֶסֶד—steadfast kindness toward Abraham. Then he proposed an extraordinary test of character: when he asked a young woman for water, the right woman would not merely give him a drink. She would voluntarily offer water to his camels as well. Genesis explicitly presents this as the servant's requested confirmation concerning the woman God had appointed for Isaac.
Then...
before he finished praying...
a woman appeared.
Her name was Rebekah.
And perhaps you already know this story so well that you are tempted to hurry through it.
Don't.
Because somewhere reading this is a person who has been praying for something that still has no visible answer.
You have prayed until your vocabulary became smaller.
At first your prayers were long.
Detailed.
Confident.
Then months passed.
Maybe years.
And now sometimes all you can manage is:
“Lord... please.”
Maybe you are praying for your marriage.
Your child.
Your family.
Direction.
Provision.
Restoration.
A prodigal who seems determined to keep running.
Freedom from something you are ashamed to admit still has a grip on you.
Maybe you are asking God whether the door should open or close.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you are doing fine, while privately you have whispered:
“God, I need You to show me that You still see me.”
Genesis 24 does not promise that every prayer will receive an immediate answer.
It does not teach us to manufacture signs, manipulate God, or turn circumstances into a superstitious code.
God is sovereign. His wisdom is higher than ours. Biblical prayer is not a technique for forcing heaven to obey our preferences.
But Genesis 24 does reveal something precious:
God can be working beyond your sight long before His answer enters your field of vision.
Think about it.
For Rebekah to appear while the servant was still speaking, she had to begin moving before he finished praying.
Her steps were already happening while his words were still happening.
The jar was already on her shoulder.
She was already approaching the place where his prayer and her ordinary day would collide.
The servant experienced the answer suddenly.
God did not begin being sovereign suddenly.
There is a difference.
And somebody needs that difference tonight.
Because you have mistaken “I cannot see God working” for “God is not working.”
Those are not the same sentence.
Faith does not mean pretending you know what God has not revealed. Faith means trusting the God who has revealed Himself even when you do not know what He is doing.
Rebekah arrives.
The servant runs toward her and asks for a little water.
She answers:
“Drink, my lord.”
And then she does exactly what he had prayed about.

She offers to draw water for the camels too. Genesis emphasizes her haste: she quickly empties her jar, runs back to the well, and keeps drawing until the camels have finished. The narrative itself highlights her generosity and hospitality.
Do not miss this.
Rebekah did not wake up that morning knowing she was walking into Genesis 24.
To her, this may have looked like another trip for water.
Another ordinary responsibility.
Another jar.
Another walk.
Another evening.
But heaven can hide enormous purposes inside ordinary obedience.
She did not need a platform.
She needed a pitcher.
She did not need to know the entire plan.
She simply needed to be the kind of woman who saw a thirsty stranger and served generously.
We spend so much time asking God for the spectacular that sometimes we underestimate the holiness of the ordinary.
The phone call you felt prompted to make.
The person you forgave.
The temptation you refused.
The meal you brought.
The truth you told when lying would have been easier.
The stranger you treated with dignity.
The prayer nobody heard.
The small obedience nobody applauded.
What if some of the most important moments of your life will not announce themselves as important?
Rebekah was carrying water.
God was carrying history.
And while she served, the servant watched her silently.

Genesis 24:21 says he observed her, waiting to learn whether the LORD had made his journey successful. Even after an astonishing apparent answer, he did not immediately explode into presumptuous certainty. He watched. He waited. More had to become clear.
There is wisdom there too.
Not everything that resembles an answer is automatically God's answer.
Discernment matters.
Scripture matters.
Character matters.
Truth matters.
God's providence will never give you permission to contradict God's revealed Word.
We should never use “God told me” as spiritual camouflage for something Scripture calls sin.
And this story is especially dangerous if we reduce it to a formula for finding a spouse.
“Ask God for a sign and the next attractive person who appears is your soulmate.”
No.
Genesis 24 is narrative, not a romantic fortune-telling technique.

This is a specific moment within the unfolding history of God's covenant promise to Abraham. The servant's prayer occurs within an assignment Abraham had already given him, and the eventual confirmation includes Rebekah's family connection, her character, her willingness, and the recognition by her household that the matter had come from the LORD.
And that makes what happens next even more beautiful.
The servant discovers who Rebekah is.
Then he bows.
Before the romance reaches Isaac, worship reaches God.
Genesis 24:26 says:
וַיִּקֹּד הָאִישׁ וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ לַיהוָה
The man bowed and worshiped the LORD.
Then he declares that God has not abandoned His חַסְדּוֹ וַאֲמִתּוֹ — chasdo va'amitto, His steadfast kindness and faithfulness toward Abraham.
Notice what the servant does when the door opens.
He does not worship the door.
He worships God.
That will preach to a generation obsessed with blessings.
We pray for the relationship.
The promotion.
The healing.
The opportunity.
The breakthrough.
The provision.
Then when it arrives, there is a subtle temptation to become more fascinated with the gift than the Giver.
But the servant's knees hit the ground.
Because answered prayer should produce worship, not entitlement.
Maybe the greatest danger is not that God never gives us what we ask for.
Maybe sometimes the danger is receiving it...
and forgetting Him.
Rebekah eventually faces a decision of her own.
Her family asks whether she will go with this man.
Genesis preserves her answer with almost shocking simplicity:
אֵלֵךְ — Elekh.
“I will go.”
Two words in English.
One Hebrew word.
A life surrendered into uncertainty.
She had not built a life with Isaac.
She had not even met him.
She was being asked to leave what was familiar and travel toward a future she could not yet see.
And she said:
Elekh.
I will go.
There are moments when faith sounds like a sermon.
And there are moments when faith is only one trembling sentence.
“I will go.”
“I forgive.”
“I surrender.”
“I confess.”
“I'll obey.”
“Jesus, save me.”
Maybe your next act of faith does not need to sound impressive.
Maybe it just needs to be real.
Because following God has always involved trusting Him beyond the edge of what we can see.
But there is something else in this story that hurts before it heals.
Isaac.
While the servant has been traveling...
while Rebekah has been drawing water...
while families have been talking...
Isaac has his own story.
His mother Sarah has died.
Genesis 23 records her death before this journey begins.
Then, at the end of Genesis 24, Isaac walks in the field toward evening and sees camels approaching.
Rebekah sees him.
He receives her as his wife.
And Scripture says:
וַיֶּאֱהָבֶהָ — vayye'ehaveha
“and he loved her.”
Then comes the line people rush past:
וַיִּנָּחֵם יִצְחָק אַחֲרֵי אִמּוֹ
Isaac was comforted after his mother.
There was grief in the love story.
An empty tent before a bride entered it.
A son carrying the absence of his mother.
A family moving forward while still remembering what had been lost.
The Bible is painfully human like that.
It does not pretend that a new blessing erases an old wound.
Rebekah did not make Sarah unimportant.
Love did not rewrite history by pretending grief never happened.
But God brought comfort into a place that had known loss.
And perhaps that is where this story finally reaches into your chest.
Because maybe you are not waiting beside the well.
Maybe you are Isaac in the field.
You lost something.
Someone.
A relationship.
A season.
A dream.
A version of yourself you thought would survive.
You have learned how to function around an empty space.
And you wonder whether joy would somehow betray what you lost.
Listen carefully:
God's comfort does not require you to pretend the wound never existed.
The God of Scripture meets real people inside real grief.
And the greater story of Scripture tells us that grief, sin, death, and brokenness do not receive the final word.
That is where Isaac and Rebekah's story must ultimately push the Christian reader beyond Isaac and Rebekah.
Because Genesis is moving somewhere.
The covenant promise is moving somewhere.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Israel.
And ultimately, through the unfolding biblical story, toward Jesus Christ.
The greatest love story in Scripture is not ultimately a man finding a woman beside a well.
It is the holy God pursuing sinners who could never rescue themselves.
We were not Rebekah impressing heaven with our generosity.
We were sinners in need of mercy.
We had rebelled.
Hidden.
Compromised.
Lusted.
Lied.
Hated.
Envied.
Worshiped ourselves.
Promised God we would stop and then returned to the same chains.
Some of us became skilled at looking Christian while secretly dying.
We knew the songs.
We knew when to say “Amen.”
We knew what verse to post.
But behind the screen...
behind the smile...
behind the Sunday clothes...
there were things we hoped nobody would ever discover.
And God already knew.
That is the scandal.
The Gospel does not begin with good people needing inspiration.
It begins with sinners needing salvation.
And God did not answer that need by sending advice.
He sent His Son.
Jesus Christ lived without sin, went willingly to the cross, bore sin, died, was buried, and rose again.
Grace is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
The cross proves it matters more terribly than we want to admit.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty people could never provide for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new life.
Not because sin was cheap.
Because Christ paid dearly.
This is why repentance is not religious self-hatred.
It is coming out of hiding.
It is agreeing with God about our sin and turning toward the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Maybe you clicked this because the title sounded romantic.
Maybe God used a love story to bring you somewhere much more personal.
What are you hiding?
What keeps returning when nobody is watching?
What have you renamed so you would not have to repent of it?
What relationship has become an idol?
What bitterness have you protected?
What secret appetite has slowly become your master?
What if the prayer you most desperately need tonight is not:
“Lord, send me my Rebekah.”
What if it is:
“Jesus, take all of me.”
Because the greatest answer God can give you is not another human being.
It is Himself.
A spouse cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
Marriage cannot forgive your sins.
Romance cannot resurrect your soul.
Only Christ saves.
Be honest before God.
You do not owe strangers the private details of your struggle. But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And if someone comes to mind while reading this, do not just think about them.
Send this to them.
And there is more than content behind this mission.
Because there may come a night when heaven feels silent and you will need to remember the servant standing beside that well.
He was praying.
Rebekah was walking.
He was speaking.
God was already working.
But remember this carefully: Genesis 24 is not a promise that every unanswered prayer has the exact answer you desire already walking toward you.
Sometimes God's answer is yes.
Sometimes no.
Sometimes wait.
Sometimes His providence takes us somewhere we never would have chosen.
Christian hope is not confidence that God will obey our script.
Christian hope is confidence that God remains faithful when we cannot read His script.
The servant could not see Rebekah until she appeared.
Rebekah could not see Isaac when she said, “I will go.”
Isaac could not see the journey taking place while he carried his grief.
Each person saw only part of the road.
God saw the whole road.
And centuries later, we can read the chapter they had to live one sentence at a time.
That may be your life right now.
You are living a sentence and demanding to understand the chapter.
You are standing beside a well asking why.
You are carrying a jar without realizing what ordinary obedience may mean.
You are crossing unfamiliar country wondering whether surrender was a mistake.
You are walking through a field carrying grief.
You see one sentence.
God sees more than you do.
So pray.
Obey what Scripture has made clear.
Refuse to manufacture signs.
Refuse to call sin “God's will.”
Refuse to make an idol out of the answer you want.
Keep walking faithfully.
Keep serving when nobody applauds.
Keep repenting when you fall.
Keep bringing your grief to Christ.
Keep your eyes on Jesus.
And when God answers differently from what you imagined, remember that the purpose of faith was never to make God the servant of your dreams.
The purpose is to know Him.
To trust Him.
To become like Christ.
To glorify Him.
Not because sharing saves you. Jesus saves.
Do it because somebody else may need the truth you almost scrolled past.
And comment something real—not something impressive.
“Jesus, I trust You while I wait.”
Maybe that is your prayer tonight.

Because somewhere between the prayer at the well, the woman carrying the jar, the grieving man in the field, and the God who saw all of them at once, Genesis leaves us with a truth difficult to forget:
You may still be speaking while God is already writing a story you cannot yet see.
And above every lesser story stands the greater one: the Savior who receives sinners, forgives the repentant, restores the broken, and turns histories marked by shame into testimonies of grace.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
